tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__delegate_task
tools.description: Start one child agent with only `task`. No parent history. Separate checkout or PR per child: `isolation:'worktree'`. Keep `taskId` for `task_status` and `task_cancel`.

options.description: Options from `orchestrator_capabilities`, such as {effort:'max'}. Given values override inherited. [] or {} clears.

isolation.description: 'shared' (default): parent checkout. 'worktree': new prepared checkout from the parent commit, for a separate checkout or PR per child. Uncommitted edits stay out.

mode.description: Default 'async'. 'wait' only if this turn needs the result. A question or approval ends the wait.

timeoutMs.description: Mode 'wait' only. Default 10 min. A timeout does not cancel the child.

runtimeMode.description: Omit unless the user asks for a supervised child. Narrow modes pause for human approval, not read-only. Above yours is rejected.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__link_pull_request
tools.description: Link a PR to this thread. T3 shows its status and settles the thread on merge.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__orchestrator_capabilities
tools.description: List providers, models, options, and runtime modes for `delegate_task`. Short list. `search` finds others. Any catalog model works.

content.thinking:
I'm planning to spawn a subagent to build the "Waiting for you" section in Overview with a toggle/filter for open chat cards like IOUs, transactions, balances, and recurring items, and push toward a PR on main — letting it run in the background rather than waiting on it.

This means I'll call orchestrator_capabilities first, then use delegate_task for background work in a separate checkout since the subagent will create a branch and PR while I only do research. When the subagent finishes, it should report back the PR URL and head SHA so I can call link_pull_request myself without babysitting the process. The toggle itself should be a collapsible section on Overview aggregating open items from every source — chat, IOUs, voice notes, calls — with possible filter chips.

I'm planning to merge IOU, transaction, balance, and recurring proposal cards into one collapsible section with filter chips (All / IOUs / Transactions / Balances / Recurring), each labeled by its source, and I'll ask the subagent to check how recurring cards currently render on Overview so they can fold in cleanly, while leaving agent run findings out since those already have their own review page. Source labeling can stay simple for now since there's no conversation ID to link back to in agent_proposals.

Next I need to dig into where voice notes would actually live — as a hold-to-record option in the chat composer, a separate quick-capture button, or tied to a call — and whether the chat backend truly supports durable/background execution, since closing the app mid-stream might kill the request depending on how the route handler and AI SDK streaming are wired. I should read through the chat route implementation closely to understand how publication, tool progress, and abort signals currently interact before deciding how to extend this to voice.

I also want to research Vercel's Workflow-based durable agents (the `@workflow/ai` DurableAgent pattern with resumable streams) as the likely foundation for a "durable chat," and separately dig into OpenAI Realtime's turn-taking mechanics — server_vad versus semantic_vad settings and how interruption/response-creation flags control when the assistant actually responds.

Beyond that, I need to understand full-duplex handling: how gpt-realtime's idle_timeout_ms works for server_vad, how conversation.item.truncate keeps the model's sense of what audio the user actually heard after an interruption, and how async function calling should be sequenced — letting the model keep talking while a tool call is pending, then deciding whether to send the function result and trigger a new response immediately or wait if the user is currently speaking, similar to how Gemini exposes SILENT/WHEN_IDLE/INTERRUPT scheduling.

There's also push-to-talk via manual turn detection and commit, noise handling through semantic_vad and near/far-field noise reduction, echo cancellation through WebRTC's built-in audio constraints, and the idea of narrating tool use — having the voice model say a preamble like "let me check the transactions" before calling a tool, informed by streamed progress events from the delegate.

I'm thinking through a progress heartbeat design: if the delegate takes more than a few seconds and the user is silent, inject a quiet update like "still checking, found 14 Netto payments so far," either as a silent context message or a brief spoken one, careful not to over-talk. I'm also comparing GPT-Live, which is purpose-built for full-duplex delegation with fast turn-taking and backchannel handling, against gpt-realtime-2.1, the more established half-duplex VAD-based model, while noting it's unclear whether the AI SDK supports the newer one yet.

I need to dig deeper into the GPT-Live delegation guide for details on client delegation mode and pricing, and also look into durable agent patterns from Vercel Workflow and AI SDK 7's resumable streams, since this matters for both voice notes and long-running tasks that continue after a call ends. For the delegation transport itself, I'm sketching how a voice session in the browser would route a tool call through the existing chat API, streaming progress back and returning the final answer as a function output, possibly via a sideband server connection to the same realtime session.

Sideband connections are more secure for server-side tool handling, but they require a persistent server connection unsuited for Vercel's serverless limits—fluid compute might stretch to 800s, but long calls could exceed that. So I'm leaning toward browser-relay as the pragmatic choice, and noting that the voice model needs clear instructions to only state numbers sourced from Moneo, keep spoken answers short, and read amounts naturally.

I'm thinking the delegate could pass a `mode: "voice"` flag so the chat agent returns short spoken sentences instead of tables, letting the voice model read responses nearly verbatim to reduce hallucination risk—though I should explicitly instruct it to quote amounts exactly rather than paraphrase. Critically, the voice model must never answer finance questions from its own memory; everything financial routes through ask_moneo, with only small talk and clarifications handled directly.

For tools, the voice model probably just needs ask_moneo and end_call, nothing else. Latency is a concern too—chit chat should feel instant while ask_moneo calls could take several seconds, so I'm considering adding a separate "voice" model entry in AI_AGENTS settings so users can pick a faster model specifically for calls.

The realtime session also needs continuity with the existing chat: injecting recent messages at session start, and for each ask_moneo call sending both the voice model's distilled request and the raw transcribed words, since the transcription and the model's interpretation of what it heard could diverge.

For storage, each turn gets saved as a chat message tagged `via: "call"`, with a summary generated afterward. For interruptions, cancelling means aborting the delegate fetch, while adding a new instruction mid-task ("also check Lidl") should reuse the existing steer endpoint rather than building something new. On iOS, I'm flagging that PWAs get suspended when backgrounded or the screen locks, so WebRTC mic access would drop — meaning locked-screen voice calls just won't work there, unlike Android.

For voice notes, Safari supports MediaRecorder in mp4/aac, so I'd upload to Supabase storage using the existing chat attachments endpoint, then transcribe and hand off to the agent. If someone closes the app mid-upload, I need the upload to complete first before allowing exit — files are small so this should be near-instant, with a "Sent ✓" confirmation gating the close action.

Thinking through the mic design, I like the idea of one button with two gestures: tap to dictate into the text box for editing, hold-and-release to send a voice note immediately like WhatsApp. If chat is durable server-side, a voice note really just becomes dictation plus auto-send, with the run continuing even if you leave the app — no separate feature needed, just durable chat with a notification when the run completes while you're away.

I'm also considering a quick entry point outside chat itself: a mic icon on Overview or an app-icon shortcut that jumps straight into recording mode. For landing behavior, the note goes to the current chat (or starts a new one if idle past 30 minutes, matching existing behavior), with resulting cards appearing in the Overview waiting section and notifications only firing if the user wasn't actively watching. I'm deciding not to keep the raw audio — just delete it after transcription and use the transcript as the message text, maybe with a small badge indicating it was a voice note. Now I need to check whether chat is currently durable by looking at how the route handles progress streaming and verified answers before publication finishes.

For background persistence, I'm weighing options: using `after()` or `waitUntil()` to keep the function alive past the response, or relying on the AI SDK's `consumeStream()` pattern so the stream continues being consumed server-side even if the client disconnects — which seems like the simplest approach without needing a full Workflow setup. I'm also considering whether a Vercel Workflow with durable execution would be needed for more complex cases.

For v1 I'll go with the simpler persistence approach since chat turns are short and well within maxDuration, and design it so reopening the app loads the persisted messages with a "working..." indicator if still running. I should check what the current route implementation actually does.

I'm also noting that for notifications, in-app alerts plus an overview section should suffice for now, with web push as a backlog item, and confirming other smaller decisions like tap-only confirmation, no cost limits, and the need for provider abstraction.

Now I'm weighing OpenAI's Realtime protocol against the AI SDK's experimental hook versus raw WebRTC, and I need to verify whether the installed AI SDK version actually supports this by checking the main repo's node_modules. I'm also thinking through audio handling details — since WebSocket transport means we manage capture and playback ourselves, I'm considering whether browser echo cancellation still functions properly without WebRTC's built-in handling.

Given that Chrome's echo cancellation historically only works with WebRTC peer connections (not WebAudio or audio playback), and OpenAI recommends WebRTC for this exact reason plus automatic interruption truncation, I'm leaning toward using WebRTC for OpenAI's best barge-in quality while reserving WebSocket for a future ElevenLabs integration. To keep things swappable despite this tradeoff, I'd abstract the app's voice session interface with connection handling and event callbacks for transcripts, tool calls, and state, so a WebSocket adapter can slot in later.

Checking the newer unified interface: it seems a server route can post the SDP offer along with session config directly to the realtime calls endpoint without needing an ephemeral token, which simplifies the server-side handshake considerably — raw WebRTC with a thin custom adapter looks better than relying on an experimental WebSocket-only hook.

I still need to dig into GPT-Live's delegation model — whether it emits a delegation event that the client resolves, which would make it purpose-built for this tool-calling pattern, plus pricing comparisons. Also want to contrast how each model decides when to speak: GPT-Live's full-duplex approach lets the model self-regulate turn-taking and handle interruptions natively, versus gpt-realtime's semantic VAD approach — worth explaining both before recommending one.

I'll start by spawning a subagent to research the delegation guide, realtime VAD docs, Vercel's durable workflow agent, iOS PWA background mic behavior, and AI SDK stream persistence on disconnect, then load the orchestrator tools.

timeoutMs.description: Mode 'wait' only. Default 10 min. A timeout does not cancel the child.

Repo: Moneo (Next.js 16 + React 19 + Supabase personal-finance app). Read AGENTS.md first and follow it: npm, simplest clean change, follow nearby patterns, one commit per logical step, run `npm test` and `npm run lint` (and `npm run build`, since this changes app UI) before opening the PR. This Next.js version differs from your training data, so check `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` before relying on any API you're unsure of.

## Goal
Cards the chat proposes (pending rows in `agent_proposals` with `run_id is null`, status `proposed` or `failed`) must be reviewable on Overview (`app/page.tsx`), not only in the chat message that created them. Today:
- `iou_create` / `iou_settle` already show on Overview via `app/iou-review.tsx` (`IouReview`, "Loans to review", uses `openIouProposals` in `lib/ai/iou-proposals.ts` and `components/iou-card`).
- Detected `recurring_edit` cards show via `app/money/recurring/review.tsx` (`RecurringReview`, rendered right after `IouReview` in `app/page.tsx`).
- `transaction_create` (`lib/ai/transaction-proposals.ts`) and `balance_set` (`lib/ai/balance-proposals.ts`) cards appear ONLY in chat. That is the gap.

Note: `app/ai/iou-actions.ts` already loads/decides proposals of kinds `iou_create, iou_settle, transaction_create, balance_set, recurring_edit`, and for an open `transaction_create` it adds account options. Find the card component chat uses for transaction/balance cards and reuse it; don't build new accept/reject logic. Applying goes through `lib/ai/agent-apply.ts` as it does now.

## What to build
One Overview section, "Waiting for you", that **collapses/expands** (the user asked for a toggle). The collapsed header shows the count of open cards. Expanded, it lists every open standalone chat card: IOUs, transactions, balances, and chat-made recurring changes. Each card keeps its existing accept/dismiss/edit behavior, using the existing card components.
- Replace the separate "Loans to review" block on Overview with this section, so loans aren't listed twice. Keep `IouReview` wherever else it's used (e.g. `app/ai/agents/page.tsx`) unless you have a clean reason to change it.
- Look at how `RecurringReview` works (it also syncs detected suggestions). If folding its cards into the same section is simple and clean, do it; if not, leave it alone and say why in the PR.
- If you can do it cheaply, add small filter chips (All / Loans / Transactions / Balances / Recurring) inside the expanded section. Otherwise skip them.
- Hide the section when there are no open cards. Default to expanded when there are cards, unless the existing UI has a clear pattern for collapsed sections (look for one, e.g. agent run review groups).
- A future voice-note feature will create cards the same way, so make this section the single place all standalone open cards appear. No voice work now.
- Keep queries scoped by `workspace_id`, `run_id is null`, status `proposed`/`failed`, with a sensible limit, oldest or newest first to match existing patterns. Add the loader in `lib/ai/` next to similar ones and memoize it with `cache` like `loadIouReview`.

## Tests
Add or adjust Vitest tests next to the existing ones (e.g. `app/home-sections.test.tsx`, `lib/ai/iou-proposals.test.ts`-style) for the new loader and the section's render (hidden when empty; lists transaction and balance cards). If a gated Playwright flow exists for Overview, run it only if Supabase/auth is configured per `e2e/README.md`; otherwise say it was skipped.

## Deliver
Branch off the current commit, commit in small steps (end each commit message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`), push, and open a PR against `main` with `gh pr create`. The PR body describes the change, the tests run and their results, and anything skipped; end it with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`. Do not merge.

Your final line must be: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>.

Search results on GPT-Live client delegation are consistent on the core mechanics, mostly from the official OpenAI docs and secondary sources.

**Event and identifiers:** The official OpenAI guide says the `session.delegation.created` event includes an `offset_ms` timestamp and delegation metadata, namely `delegation.id` and `delegation.target` (developers.openai.com, "Delegation and tools in GPT-Live"). The Microsoft Foundry reference adds that the `delegation` object carries id, type, and target, and that a null or omitted delegation selects client mode.

**No task text:** The event deliberately omits what the user asked for. The OpenAI guide says it does not contain the utterance, so the app must rebuild the request from transcript events and its own state. The app should save `delegation.id` and use it to correlate later updates.

**Replies:** Per the OpenAI migration guide and the Evalgent write-up, the app runs its own backend and sends back `session.commentary.append` with the `delegation_id`. The Hands-on post describes `session.thinking.append` as context the model should know but not necessarily say. Note that `session.instructions.append` also exists in the Microsoft reference.

**Setup:** Client mode is set with `delegation: {type: "client"}` at session creation. The mode is fixed for the session, so switching requires a new session.

**Caveats:** The OpenAI guide and Foundry docs describe the same mechanics. The GitHub issue and blog posts are secondary and some use model names and details that I could not verify against the official docs. I did not find the `developers.openai.com` page covering `thinking` or `commentary` append semantics in detail, so check that page directly for exact payload fields and any limits such as the roughly 500-token guidance mentioned in a GitHub issue.

# Prompting GPT-Live: Summary

**Delegation.** Tell GPT-Live when to hand work to the backend, and use the trigger phrase `Generate <|SpawnThinking|>`. The page advises against "delegate to the backend" wording. The recommended `Delegation policy` lists backend capabilities under "Backend tools" and gives concrete conditions under "Generate <|SpawnThinking|> when" and "Do not generate <|SpawnThinking|> when." Its example includes "The user asks to change a booking." The page also says "Generate <|SpawnThinking|> before giving an answer that depends on backend work," and "Do not guess the result while waiting."

**Narration ("let me check...").** The page does not give a fixed script for this. A spoken acknowledgment is not a confirmation: "A spoken promise such as “I’m checking that” does not confirm that backend work has started." The prompt should request delegation through `<|SpawnThinking|>`. For progress updates, the page points to `session.commentary.append`. Tool-call chattiness is a personality choice: one example gives only "Okay, looking it up." and then stays silent, while a chattier one gives short progress updates.

**Silence.** Pauses are not new requests. Use an instruction such as "Keep listening while the user pauses to think." Also: "Do not treat a cough, music, or nearby conversation as a new request."

**Interruptions.** Use "Stop speaking when the user interrupts." The page warns that GPT-Live "may keep speaking briefly after an interruption," so test short and long interjections with your chosen voice. Stopping speech does not stop work: "Stopping speech leaves backend work running." If the user changes the task, update the application's active work too.

**Backchannels.** These are brief listening sounds such as "mm-hmm." The backchannel policy controls frequency, from none ("Backchanneling is entirely disallowed") to "Frequent" or "Very frequent." Tune them separately from acknowledgments. To keep them during interruptions, avoid rules that forbid all overlapping speech.

**Numbers, amounts, and confirmations.** The page says to "wait for the backend’s result before stating a price, confirming a booking." For unclear details, "Ask a focused clarification when an important name, date, or number is unclear," and "Do not guess the missing value." Confirmations are enforced outside the model: "Your application checks permissions and required confirmations before executing an action."

**Prompt structure.** Start from the template, keep its three headings (Backchannel policy, Interruption policy, Delegation policy), and customize the text under each. Keep the role and speaking-style lines at the top. List backend capabilities, and put full task procedures in backend instructions. Test the simpler prompt on representative conversations as you revise it. Optional controls (response length, language, translation, selective responses, and so on) should be added only when testing shows a need.

# Client delegation in GPT-Live: technical summary

## Setup

Client delegation is selected when the session is created with `delegation: { type: "client" }`. To change modes, the page says you must "start a new session." Your application chooses the backend model or service, instructions, tools, and routing.

## Events

| Event | Direction | Key fields | Effect on speech |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session.delegation.created` | Server → client | `offset_ms`, `delegation.id`, `delegation.type`, `delegation.target` (`"client"`) | Metadata only. Not spoken. |
| `session.commentary.append` | Client → server | `event_id`, `delegation_id`, `content` | Content the model should say aloud. The model may paraphrase it: "it is trained to paraphrase the text." |
| `session.thinking.append` | Client → server | `event_id`, `delegation_id`, `content` | Used for later replies without being said when it arrives. |
| `session.instructions.append` | Client → server | `event_id`, `delegation_id` (`null` for session-wide), `content` | Steers the live model. It can interrupt current speech or behavior. |

Each append has an acknowledgment that echoes your `event_id` as `client_event_id`: `session.commentary.appended`, `session.thinking.appended`, or `session.instructions.appended`. The page says the acknowledgment "waits for estimated context injection, not for speech or playback to finish."

Example shape (illustrative, not from the page):

```json
{
  "type": "session.commentary.append",
  "event_id": "result_2",
  "delegation_id": "<id from session.delegation.created>",
  "content": "Your table is booked for 7 PM on Friday."
}
```

**Limits:** `content` is a plain string of up to 500 tokens per append. A non-null `delegation_id` must match a known client delegation. You can send multiple updates under the same ID.

## Progress vs. final results

- **Progress:** Use `session.thinking.append` for quiet status, such as "Checking Thursday availability. No appointment has been booked."
- **Final or spoken results:** Use `session.commentary.append`, and only after the backend confirms success. The page says to "Report an action as complete after the tool or service confirms success."
- **Session-wide guidance:** Use `session.instructions.append` with `delegation_id: null`. Example use: after a guardrail blocks a request, redirect the conversation. The page notes that "The instruction does not cancel backend work."

## Reconstructing the task from transcripts

- Collect `session.input_transcript.delta` and `session.output_transcript.delta`. Each carries `delta`, `start_ms`, and `end_ms`.
- Keep enough history to interpret short replies such as "yes" or corrections.
- Fragments are not complete turns, and transcripts "may contain mistakes."
- The delegation event contains "metadata, not task text," so the task must come from transcripts and application state.
- Save `delegation.id` and include it unchanged in every update for that task.

## Cancellation and concurrency

- Interrupting speech does not stop backend work: "Interrupting the spoken conversation leaves backend work running."
- Cancel in your backend, and confirm cancellation before telling the user it happened.
- Track each action with an operation ID and each changed request with a task revision, alongside the delegation ID. Discard results for outdated requests, such as a Friday request after the user changed it to Thursday.
- Before retrying, check whether the original action already happened, so a lost response doesn't cause a duplicate booking.
- **Acknowledgment side effect:** Any thinking or commentary append "cancels all pending automatic acknowledgments in the session, including those for other delegations."

## Suppressing automatic acknowledgments

1. Set `delegation.acknowledgement_delay_ms` at session creation (the page's example uses `800`).
2. On receiving `session.delegation.created`, immediately send `session.thinking.append` with empty `content` and that delegation's ID.
3. Send the verified result later with `session.commentary.append`.

The page warns that this does not guarantee silence. The model may still speak earlier, so use application-controlled playback when silence must be guaranteed.

## Function tools

The page does not say GPT-Live executes function tools directly in client mode. Client mode means your application "configures and runs the backend," including its tools. Function calling, `function_call_output` items, and `response.create` continuation are described for Responses delegation, where your application executes custom functions and returns results.

## Confirmation and approval

The page assigns these to your application: "Enforce permissions and required confirmations in your application." Check permissions and required confirmations before running work, and before announcing actions as done.

## Size and payload guidance

- Keep to 500 tokens per append.
- Keep large structured payloads, long tool output, and display Markdown in the backend.
- Send facts and brief summaries, not "private backend reasoning" or secrets.

- **Suspension is the core problem.** An Apple Developer Forums post requests background WebRTC for audio apps, noting that Safari suspends these technologies once the screen locks or the browser goes to the background ([developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774239](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774239)).
- **Home-screen web apps are affected.** A WebKit bug from October 2024 reports that the microphone works in Safari but stops working when the app is added to the Home Screen ([bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=226620](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=226620)).
- **Locking the screen can mute the mic.** A 2022 WebKit report describes the microphone turning off after the iPhone locks during a WebRTC meeting ([bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=241400](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=241400)).

A blog post suggests the Wake Lock API and standalone mode reduce interruptions but don't fully fix them ([rss.boorghani.com/?p=388696](https://rss.boorghani.com/?p=388696)).

- **semantic_vad and eagerness:** OpenAI's guide says Semantic VAD can be activated by setting session.audio.input.turn_detection.type to semantic_vad. Now I'm thinking through who controls turn-taking: with GPT-Live the model itself decides via full-duplex behavior shaped by prompt sections like backchannel, interruption, and delegation policies, whereas gpt-realtime-2.x relies on VAD settings like semantic_vad eagerness. I'm leaning toward recommending GPT-Live paired with careful prompting so we retain control over what it says during work.

For the specific policies, I'm settling on light defaults: occasional backchannels, immediate stop-speaking on interruption while work continues in background, and patient listening during pauses without reacting to coughs or background noise. For narration while working, I'm mapping tool names from the existing NDJSON tool-progress stream to spoken phrases — like finance_investigate becoming "searching your transactions" or forecast_evaluate becoming "running the forecast" — so the assistant can announce what it's doing in real time as delegation events fire.

For the final answer, since chat returns Markdown but voice needs a short spoken version, I'm thinking of either adding a system prompt instruction telling the agent this is a voice call and to lead with a brief spoken summary, or simpler, stripping card/chart blocks from the text and sending the remainder as commentary while instructing exact number pronunciation. For reconstructing the task description since delegation events carry no text, I plan to gather the transcript since the last delegation (recent user and assistant turns) and pass that as the message to the chat endpoint, framed as coming from a voice call.

Since the chat route pulls conversation history from the DB, I realize voice turns need to be persisted as messages so the agent actually sees them, meaning I should send the user's words since the last delegation plus a few recent spoken exchanges as bounded context, tagged with a `via: "call"` marker. For handling corrections mid-task, like the user changing their mind partway through, I'm considering using the existing steer endpoint to redirect a running request rather than canceling and restarting it.

For cancellation, I think a manual UI cancel button is simplest since the agent can't cleanly cancel itself mid-flight, while voice-based corrections ("never mind", "stop that") can route through steering. Confirmation happens only visually (never by voice) once something lands in the tray or Overview, and since there are no call duration limits, I'm leaving silence/end handling to a manual end-call button rather than auto-ending, keeping in mind billing accrues per second while the call is live.

content.text:
The subagent is building the Overview "Waiting for you" section and will open a PR against `main`. I won't wait on it: <t3-thread://v2/88042f69-c439-49f6-a4b9-1fb5180f2502/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3A3f8ee9f3-e93b-4650-aafd-a0e03df88d87%3Adelegate-task%3Aed1f0c9e-c82e-46dd-846c-88252d531d88>. The "later" items are now in `BACKLOG.md` (commit `fd362e09` on this branch, not pushed).

Here is the plan after the deeper research.

## Correction to what I said before

- **OpenAI now has a model built exactly for this: GPT-Live.** It listens while it talks, decides itself when to hand work to a backend, and keeps talking while that work runs. That backend is our Moneo agent. It costs $0.05 per minute of call, plus Luna's normal token cost.
- **We already have it installed.** Our `@ai-sdk/openai` already supports `gpt-live-1` with hand-off to our own agent. The server sets up the call, so your OpenAI key never reaches the browser.
- **Swapping providers costs more than I said.** GPT-Live uses its own protocol; ElevenLabs copies OpenAI's older Realtime protocol. Adding ElevenLabs later would take a day or two, not a one-line change. We keep that possible by having the call screen only deal with "here's a task, here's the answer."

## "When does it answer?" GPT-Live decides that itself

There is no "wait N ms of silence, then reply" setting. It hears you continuously and picks its moment. We steer it with three short sections in its instructions and with what we send back.

| Behavior | What we set |
|---|---|
| Little listening sounds ("mm-hm") | Occasional |
| You interrupt it | It stops talking; Moneo's work keeps running |
| You pause to think, cough, background noise | Keep listening; not a new request |
| Before giving any number | Always ask Moneo; never guess or state an amount itself |
| While Moneo works | Speaks short updates, for example "let me look through your transactions…" |
| Unclear name, amount or date | Asks one short question instead of guessing |

The narration you asked for works because our chat route already reports each tool as it starts. We turn those into short spoken lines ("searching your transactions", "running the forecast", "putting that on a card"):
- The first update is said out loud.
- Later ones are passed quietly, and it speaks one only if the wait is long and you're silent.
- The final answer is said out loud, and only after Moneo has actually finished.

## How one request flows during a call

1. You say "how much did I spend at Netto this month?"
2. GPT-Live says something like "let me check" and hands the task to Moneo. The hand-off contains no text, so our app builds the request from your transcribed words plus the last few exchanges.
3. The browser sends that to the **existing `/api/chat`**, marked as coming from a call, in the same conversation. Same Luna, same tools, same rules.
4. While it runs, the call screen shows the activity line and spoken updates. Any cards drop into the tray and into Overview's "Waiting for you".
5. When Moneo finishes, a short spoken version of its answer goes back to GPT-Live (it accepts about 500 tokens). Moneo answers in a few plain sentences for calls, while charts and cards still appear on screen.
6. If you change your mind mid-task ("no, Lidl"), it goes through the **existing steer feature** for the running request, and results for the outdated request are dropped.
7. After you hang up, the chat shows a call summary card with the full transcript collapsed inside it. The Moneo turns from the call are already saved as normal chat messages.

## Where the voice note lives: the same mic as dictation

| Gesture | Result |
|---|---|
| **Tap** the mic | Dictation. Text appears in the input box; you edit and send. Works in chat, artifacts, anywhere you can type. |
| **Hold** the mic (release to send, slide to cancel, like WhatsApp) | Voice note. Sent right away into the current chat with a 🎙 badge. You can close the app. Cards go to Overview, plus a notification. |
| Extra entry point | A "voice note" button on Overview opens chat and starts recording straight away. |

So a voice note isn't a separate feature; it's a message sent by voice. But you spotted the real blocker: **today a chat run stops when you close the app.** The route ties the work to the browser connection and cancels on disconnect (`app/api/chat/route.ts:204` and `:310`).

The fix I recommend is small: run the work with Next's `after()` so it keeps going after you leave, and stop it only via the existing cancel endpoint. Answers are already saved when a run finishes, so reopening the chat just shows them. It also helps normal chat (close mid-answer and the answer is still there) and calls (hang up mid-task and the cards still arrive).

The full Workflow-based version would survive crashes and very long runs, but it's a big rewrite of the chat route and its per-user database access. Chat turns are already capped at 90 seconds, so that one is in the backlog.

Speech-to-text runs on our server with OpenAI's transcription model. We give it your account, merchant and category names so "Netto" and "Revolut" come out right. The audio is never stored.

## Two limits to accept

- **iPhone:** web apps lose the microphone when the screen locks or you switch apps, so a call only lasts while Moneo is open on screen. We keep the screen awake during calls. Voice notes are fine because the upload takes about a second. A native wrapper is in the backlog.
- **Cost:** you said no limits. Note that an open call bills even while silent: $3 an hour.

## Recommended build order (one PR per step)

1. **Overview "Waiting for you"** (in progress with the subagent).
2. **Chat runs keep going after you close the app**, using `after()`, plus a notification when a run finishes with nobody watching.
3. **Mic**: tap to dictate, hold for a voice note, plus a transcription route that knows your merchant names.
4. **Call**: the call setup route, the hand-off loop into `/api/chat`, short spoken answers for calls, and the call screen (orb, captions, spoken and visual activity, card tray, mute, end, plus a text box for typing an exact amount).
5. **After the call**: summary card and transcript, and a separate "voice" model setting that defaults to your chat model, so you can pick a faster one for calls if Luna feels slow.

Shall I start on step 2 once the subagent's PR is up?

The user pasted their own API key directly into chat, which means it's now sitting in this conversation's transcript. The appropriate move is just to store it in .env so it stays out of version control, while quietly noting they may want to rotate it later since it's been exposed in the chat log.

I need to check whether this worktree already has a .env, and whether the main repo's .env only has the OpenRouter key — if so, I'll add OPENAI_API_KEY here, copying the main .env as a base if this worktree lacks one, without touching the main checkout directly. I should also update the stored memory notes about OpenRouter-only keys now that an OpenAI key exists, and flag that some tests needing OPENAI_API_KEY may still fail if vitest doesn't load .env automatically.

Separately, the user wants a cascaded speech-to-text/LLM/text-to-speech mode with ElevenLabs voices that has the same call capabilities, which I should add to the backlog. They also raised the question of handling multiple concurrent tasks during a call — one request being checked while another starts, with answers spoken independently as each resolves. That requires figuring out whether the chat route allows truly concurrent requests per conversation or serializes them, since steering a second task into the first wouldn't give the independent, parallel behavior the user actually wants.

Thinking through delegation IDs and commentary appends, I note that any commentary cancels all pending acknowledgments across delegations. The harder problem is message ordering when parallel tasks write to the same conversation — a second task won't see the first's result, which is fine for independent questions but not for dependent ones like "and add that to...". Since the backend can't easily distinguish a correction from a new independent task, I'm leaning toward treating every new utterance as a new parallel delegation while feeding the agent context about other currently-running tasks, though corrections like "no, Lidl" would still spawn a stale duplicate that needs handling.

Since GPT-Live retains conversation context, it can naturally handle corrections by noting which results are stale when they arrive—so I'll make each request its own parallel task, label results clearly, and let GPT-Live decide what to mention, plus add a cancel button per task as a fallback. As for timing, I'm unsure whether injected results get spoken immediately or wait for a natural pause—probably the model handles that judgment itself, so the app likely just needs to inject the commentary and trust GPT-Live's timing.

On the tap-vs-hold mic question, the user's feedback suggests having two different gestures trigger different behaviors is confusing, so I'm now considering collapsing this into a single consistent mic action rather than distinguishing tap from hold.

Simplify: during recording show two buttons, Stop (lands in box to edit) and Send (sends directly) — one entry point with a choice at the end, no confusing gestures. I should also check whether artifact generation stays durable when leaving the app, likely by looking at how the artifacts route streams generation.

For process, I need to push this branch to origin so subagent PRs can target it, with me reviewing and merging. Since the user wants to keep talking but already agreed with the durability fix, I can kick off that work via a subagent in parallel while we continue discussing the open questions like concurrent tasks design and the mic gesture.

I'm also thinking about PR #118, which targets main directly as explicitly requested earlier — I should merge its branch into t3/92af81d7 so the integration branch contains everything cleanly, avoiding conflicts once #118 merges to main. Then I'll check on the .env setup, chat concurrency handling, and artifact generation.

input.task:
Repo: Moneo (Next.js 16 + React 19 + Supabase personal-finance app). Read AGENTS.md first and follow it: npm, simplest clean change, follow nearby patterns, one commit per logical step. Run `npm test`, `npm run lint` and `npm run build` before opening the PR. This Next.js version differs from your training data: read `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/04-functions/after.md` and the `maxDuration` route segment config doc before using them. For the gated Playwright flows, copy the git-ignored `C:\codebases\Moneo\.env` into your checkout and follow `e2e/README.md`. Run them only if port 3000 is free; never print secrets.

## Goal
A chat answer or an artifact build keeps running on the server when the user closes the tab, locks the phone or navigates away. When they come back, the result is there. Only an explicit cancel stops a run. This is the base for voice notes (speak, send, close the app) and voice calls (hang up while work is running).

## Today
- `app/api/chat/route.ts` ties the run to the HTTP request. `streamText` gets `abortSignal: AbortSignal.any([request.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(90_000)])` (~line 204), there are several `if (request.signal.aborted) throw ...` checks (~lines 73, 118, 144, 243, 297), and the catch calls `cancel_chat_request` when the request was aborted (~line 310). Closing the app therefore cancels the run. The NDJSON stream already writes in a try/catch ("the reader went away; work continues"), and `finish_chat_request` already persists the answer to `messages`.
- Explicit cancel already exists: `PATCH /api/chat` calls the `cancel_chat_request` RPC (see `supabase/migrations/202610010023_chat_requests.sql`; `chat_requests.status` is running/completed/failed/canceled). Steering already reads the DB once per model step via `take_chat_steers` (~line 212).
- `app/api/artifacts/route.ts` (`maxDuration = 300`) runs `generateText` with `abortSignal: AbortSignal.any([request.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(280_000)])`, so it has the same problem.

## Build
1. **Chat:** decouple the run from `request.signal`. Keep the work alive after the response or connection ends using Next's `after()` (or whatever the docs say is right for a streaming route handler). Set a suitable `maxDuration` on the chat route. Cancellation comes only from the explicit cancel. The running run should notice it (e.g. check `chat_requests.status` at the existing per-step point, then abort through its own AbortController) and must not overwrite a canceled request. Keep the 90s timeout. Keep the existing safety re-checks (workspace unchanged, AI scope still allowed) before publishing.
2. **Coming back to a running chat:** find how the client loads a conversation (`lib/ai/use-chat-request.ts`, `lib/ai/selected-conversation.ts`, `lib/ai/conversation-history.ts`, `app/api/conversations/[id]`). If a request in that conversation is still `running`, show it as working (reuse the existing in-progress UI) and show the answer once it completes. Simple polling is fine; skip resumable streams.
3. **Artifacts:** same treatment. A build keeps going after the user leaves, cancels only explicitly (add a cancel path only if one exists or is trivially needed), and on return the user sees it running or finished. Follow how artifacts are stored and loaded today.
4. **Attention:** open cards a background run created must be findable later. Overview's "Waiting for you" section (`lib/ai/open-proposals.ts`) already lists them. Check how the bell / `/ai/activity?filter=attention` feed is built. If it can cheaply show "a chat finished while you were away, with N new cards", add that; if not, explain why in the PR. No web push.

## Tests
Add or adjust Vitest tests next to the existing ones (`app/api/chat/route.test.ts` and similar):
- a client disconnect no longer cancels or fails the run, and it still finishes and persists;
- an explicit cancel stops it and isn't overwritten;
- the artifact route behaves the same way.

## Deliver
Branch off your checkout's current commit (it is `t3/voice-finance-agent`). Commit in small steps; end each commit message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Push and open a PR with `gh pr create --base t3/voice-finance-agent`. **Do not target main.** The PR body explains the change, the tests run with their results, and anything skipped; end it with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`. Do not merge. Ignore the "Entire Gates" approval check.

Your final line must be: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking through how to handle multiple simultaneous tasks: each request runs as its own parallel task with no shared lock, and GPT-Live can track multiple delegations by ID. I'm sketching the flow and rules—giving each task a short spoken label like "checking Netto" then "checking Lidl too," and making sure results are spoken in arrival order without interrupting an ongoing sentence.

For corrections like "actually make it Lidl," I'm deciding whether GPT-Live should infer from context or auto-cancel the old task—leaning toward context inference plus a manual ✕ to cancel from the activity list. For dependent tasks like "add that to my spending," I'm simplifying by having each new task see the list of running and finished tasks, so Moneo can reference already-completed results or state it's waiting if something isn't done yet, rather than trying to detect dependencies explicitly. Writes from parallel tasks stay independent, each surfaced as its own tap-only card.

Now I'm thinking about capping concurrent tasks—maybe 3 running at once—and the mic gesture behavior: should tap and hold do the same thing to avoid confusion? I'm weighing three options: (A) tap opens a recording screen with live waveform/text and separate Send/Stop buttons, treating tap and hold identically; (B) mic always sends immediately on release, voice-first and fast, relying on cards to catch errors; (C) mic always fills the text box for manual editing before sending, classic dictation style.

I'm also considering streaming transcription (live words appearing as you speak) versus uploading after you stop recording—streaming feels cooler but uploading after is simpler for v1, and either way durability is a concern if the app closes mid-recording. I'll keep my answer compact and then ask the user 2-3 questions covering mic behavior, how to handle concurrent task corrections, and the max parallel task limit.

Step 2 is running in the background, opening a PR into `t3/voice-finance-agent` that also includes PR #118; I've noted your OpenAI key is now exposed in the chat log and should be rotated once things work, and added ElevenLabs/separate STT-TTS to the backlog. I'll continue detailing how parallel call handling and the two design decisions work.

Repo: Moneo (Next.js 16 + React 19 + Supabase personal-finance app, AI SDK 7 with `@ai-sdk/openai`). Read AGENTS.md first and follow it: npm, simplest clean change, follow nearby patterns, Zod for input, one commit per logical step. Run `npm test`, `npm run lint` and `npm run build` before opening the PR. This Next.js version differs from your training data, so check `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` for any API you're unsure of. For the gated Playwright flows, copy the git-ignored `C:\codebases\Moneo\.env` (it has `OPENAI_API_KEY`) into your checkout. Run them only if port 3000 is free; never print secrets.

## Goal: one mic button for voice input
The user wants a single mic that behaves the same whether you tap it or hold it. No gesture differences.
1. Press the mic and recording starts. **Your words appear live** while you speak, together with a level or waveform indicator.
2. Two buttons while recording:
   - **Send**: sends the message straight away as a normal chat message, marked as spoken (e.g. a small mic badge, via the message `context`). The user may close the app right after; another branch is making chat runs keep going after the client disconnects, so don't build that here.
   - **Done**: stops and puts the text into the input box to edit before sending.
   - Also a way to cancel and discard.
3. The mic goes in the chat composer (`app/ai/chat-form.tsx` and whatever composer chat uses) and in the artifact request input(s) under `app/ai/artifacts`. In an artifact input, Send submits that input.
4. Add a small "Voice note" button on Overview (`app/page.tsx` header area). It opens chat with the mic already recording (e.g. `/ai?voice=1`), so a quick spoken expense ("spent 12.40 cash at Netto, chips and eggs") is one tap away. The chat agent already turns that into `transaction_propose` cards, which show on Overview's "Waiting for you".

## Transcription
- The OpenAI key must stay on the server. Live words need streaming transcription. Look at what the installed AI SDK supports first: `@ai-sdk/openai` `experimental_realtime`, the realtime transcription session with model ids like `gpt-realtime-whisper` / `gpt-4o-transcribe`, and the `TranscriptionModelV4Stream*` types in `@ai-sdk/provider`. Then pick the simplest robust approach. Example: a route handler that creates a short-lived OpenAI realtime *transcription* session or client secret for the browser, with WebRTC or WebSocket from the browser. A server-relayed stream is fine if simpler. Fall back to upload-then-transcribe only if live isn't practical, and say so in the PR.
- Improve accuracy by passing a transcription prompt or vocabulary with the workspace's account, category and frequent merchant names (scoped by `workspace_id`, small and bounded). Reuse existing loaders where possible.
- Auth: require the signed-in workspace (`requireWorkspace`), validate input with Zod, and limit recording length to something sane (e.g. 2 minutes).
- Never store raw audio. The transcript text is what gets sent.
- Handle mic permission denied and an unsupported browser gracefully. Safari/iOS needs `getUserMedia` called from the user's tap. Keep the UI accessible (labels, focus, `aria-live` for the live text).

## Tests
Vitest tests next to existing ones for:
- the session/transcription route: auth, validation, vocabulary scoping;
- the composer's state machine: idle → recording → Send / Done / cancel. Mock the browser audio pieces.

## Deliver
Branch off your checkout's current commit (it is `t3/voice-finance-agent`). Commit in small steps; end each commit message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Push and open a PR with `gh pr create --base t3/voice-finance-agent`. **Do not target main.** The PR body explains the approach chosen for live transcription and why, the tests run with their results, and anything skipped; end it with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`. Do not merge. Ignore the "Entire Gates" approval check.

Your final line must be: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>.

---
name: voice-design-decisions
description: Agreed design for Moneo voice (mic, voice notes, GPT-Live calls) as of 2026-10-30
metadata:
  type: project
---

Agreed with the user on 2026-10-29/30 for the voice feature (built on [[voice-feature-branch-workflow]]):
- Calls: OpenAI GPT-Live (`gpt-live-1`, $0.05/min) with client delegation. GPT-Live talks; every real request goes to the existing `/api/chat` Moneo agent (user's chat model, GPT-6 Luna) in the same conversation. WebRTC set up server-side via `@ai-sdk/openai` live support, so the key never reaches the browser.
- While Moneo works, it says what it's doing out loud ("let me look through your transactions"), not only on screen.
- Several tasks at once: each request is its own parallel task, with **no limit**. Results are spoken as they arrive, held while the user is mid-sentence. Corrections: GPT-Live judges whether an old result is stale; each task has an ✕ to stop it.
- Confirm is tap-only on cards (tray during the call, and Overview "Waiting for you"). Voice never accepts.
- Mic: one button, same for tap or hold, with live words. At the end you choose **Send** (goes now; you can close the app) or **Done** (edit in the box). A voice note is just a spoken message, not a separate feature.
- Chat and artifact runs must keep going after the app is closed (Next `after()`, cancel only explicitly).
- After a call: summary card plus collapsible transcript in the chat. Both phone and desktop matter. No cost limits for now.
- Later items are in BACKLOG.md "Voice: later" (ElevenLabs, separate speech-to-text and text-to-speech pipeline, discreet mode, etc.).

**Why:** the user wants the coolest real voice agent, but with financial truth staying in app code.
**How to apply:** build steps against these decisions; ask before changing any of them.

Repo: Moneo (Next.js 16 + React 19 + Supabase personal-finance app, AI SDK 7 with `@ai-sdk/openai`). ## Goal: one mic button for voice input
The user wants a single mic that behaves the same whether you tap it or hold it. No gesture differences.
1. Press the mic and recording starts. **Your words appear live** while you speak, together with a level or waveform indicator.
2. Two buttons while recording:
   - **Send**: sends the message straight away as a normal chat message, marked as spoken (e.g. a small mic badge, via the message `context`). The user may close the app right after; another branch is making chat runs keep going after the client disconnects, so don't build that here.
   - **Done**: stops and puts the text into the input box to edit before sending.
   - Also a way to cancel and discard.
3. The mic goes in the chat composer (`app/ai/chat-form.tsx` and whatever composer chat uses) and in the artifact request input(s) under `app/ai/artifacts`. In an artifact input, Send submits that input.
4. Add a small "Voice note" button on Overview (`app/page.tsx` header area). It opens chat with the mic already recording (e.g. `/ai?voice=1`), so a quick spoken expense ("spent 12.40 cash at Netto, chips and eggs") is one tap away. The chat agent already turns that into `transaction_propose` cards, which show on Overview's "Waiting for you".

## Transcription
- The OpenAI key must stay on the server. Live words need streaming transcription. Look at what the installed AI SDK supports first: `@ai-sdk/openai` `experimental_realtime`, the realtime transcription session with model ids like `gpt-realtime-whisper` / `gpt-4o-transcribe`, and the `TranscriptionModelV4Stream*` types in `@ai-sdk/provider`. Then pick the simplest robust approach. Example: a route handler that creates a short-lived OpenAI realtime *transcription* session or client secret for the browser, with WebRTC or WebSocket from the browser. A server-relayed stream is fine if simpler. Fall back to upload-then-transcribe only if live isn't practical, and say so in the PR.
- Improve accuracy by passing a transcription prompt or vocabulary with the workspace's account, category and frequent merchant names (scoped by `workspace_id`, small and bounded). Reuse existing loaders where possible.
- Auth: require the signed-in workspace (`requireWorkspace`), validate input with Zod, and limit recording length to something sane (e.g. 2 minutes).
- Never store raw audio. The transcript text is what gets sent.
- Handle mic permission denied and an unsupported browser gracefully. Safari/iOS needs `getUserMedia` called from the user's tap. Keep the UI accessible (labels, focus, `aria-live` for the live text).

## Tests
Vitest tests next to existing ones for:
- the session/transcription route: auth, validation, vocabulary scoping;
- the composer's state machine: idle → recording → Send / Done / cancel. Mock the browser audio pieces.
